claim: More than 25 million people in the United States suffer daily from severe pain.
source: Pain affects almost every person at some point in their lives, and it has been estimated that more than 25 million people in the United States suffer daily from severe pain (Nahin, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Nahin, 2015.

claim: Approximately 80% of opioid addicts reported initiating their habit through prescription opioids.
source: As the use of opioid analgesics increased and then came under greater restrictions, so too has their diversion, misuse, and switch to illicit opioids, as ~80% of opioid addicts reported initiating their habit through prescription opioids.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text without specific citation.

claim: The epidemic of opioid abuse caused more than 47,600 deaths in 2017 alone.
source: The epidemic of opioid abuse caused more than 47,600 deaths in 2017 alone, (Overdose Death Rates, 2019) making drug overdose the leading cause of accidental death in the US.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Overdose Death Rates, 2019.

claim: Drug overdose is the leading cause of accidental death in the US.
source: The epidemic of opioid abuse caused more than 47,600 deaths in 2017 alone, (Overdose Death Rates, 2019) making drug overdose the leading cause of accidental death in the US.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Overdose Death Rates, 2019.

claim: Opioid ligands showing a preference for activating only G protein-mediated signal transduction pathways will demonstrate diminished side effects.
source: It has been proposed that opioid ligands showing a preference (bias) for activating only G protein-mediated signal transduction pathways, or against recruiting βarrestin-2, will demonstrate diminished side effects (Raehal and Bohn, 2011; Chiang et al., 2016; Majumdar and Devi, 2018; Faouzi et al., 2020a).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Oliceridine (TRV130) has been recently approved by the FDA.
source: The first biased ligand, a MOR biased agonist oliceridine (TRV130) (DeWire et al., 2013) has been recently approved by the FDA (FDA Approves New Opioid for Intravenous Use in Hospitals, 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to FDA approval documentation.

claim: TRV130 displays weak G-protein bias in vitro.
source: It is important to note, however, that TRV130 displays weak G-protein bias in vitro (Schmid et al., 2017) and mixed safety results in rodent models (Austin Zamarripa et al., 2018; Altarifi et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Schmid et al., 2017.

claim: SR17018 shows diminished respiratory depression in rodents compared to fentanyl.
source: Other MOR ligands with greater bias, such as SR17018 (Schmid et al., 2017), show diminished respiratory depression in rodents compared to fentanyl (Gillis et al., 2020a)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Gillis et al., 2020a.

claim: PZM21 and mitragynine(s) display reduced abuse liability.
source: while PZM21 (Manglik et al., 2016; Kudla et al., 2019) and mitragynine(s) (Váradi et al., 2016; Kruegel et al., 2016; Kruegel et al., 2019; Chakraborty and Majumdar, 2020) display reduced abuse liability (Yue et al., 2018; Hemby et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Some KOR-selective G protein biased ligands show a promising separation of place aversion from analgesia.
source: Similarly, some KOR-selective G protein biased ligands such as HS666 (Spetea et al., 2017), 6′GNTI (Rives et al., 2012), and triazole 1.1 (Brust et al., 2016) show a promising separation of place aversion from analgesia, unlike balanced KOR agonists.
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: RB64, HS665, and collybolide retain the aversive properties of balanced KOR agonists despite being G protein biased.
source: On the other hand, other KOR ligands such as RB64 (White et al., 2015), HS665 (Spetea et al., 2017), and collybolide (Gupta et al., 2016) retain the aversive properties of balanced KOR agonists despite being G protein biased.
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Simultaneous activation of MOR and KOR may produce synergistic analgesia while the contrasting side-effects offset respective liabilities.
source: Prior evidence shows that simultaneous activation of MOR and KOR may produce synergistic analgesia, while the contrasting side-effects offset respective liabilities (Sutters et al., 1990; Pan, 1998).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Sutters et al., 1990 and Pan, 1998.

claim: KOR agonists such as U50,488h show no sign of respiratory depression on their own.
source: For example, KOR agonists such as U50,488h, while showing no sign of respiratory depression on their own, Matthes et al., 1998 have been reported to reduce the respiratory depression mediated by icv administration of DAMGO (Dosaka-Akita et al., 1993; Haji and Takeda, 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Matthes et al., 1998.

claim: U50,488h has been reported to reduce the respiratory depression mediated by icv administration of DAMGO.
source: For example, KOR agonists such as U50,488h, while showing no sign of respiratory depression on their own, Matthes et al., 1998 have been reported to reduce the respiratory depression mediated by icv administration of DAMGO (Dosaka-Akita et al., 1993; Haji and Takeda, 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Dosaka-Akita et al., 1993 and Haji and Takeda, 2001.

claim: Nalbuphine is a moderate efficacy MOR partial agonist and high efficacy KOR partial agonist.
source: Likewise, nalbuphine, a moderate efficacy MOR partial agonist and high efficacy KOR partial agonist (Schmidt et al., 1985; Peng et al., 2007), is similar in analgesic efficacy to morphine, but shows negligible respiratory effects (Schmidt et al., 1985)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Schmidt et al., 1985 and Peng et al., 2007.

claim: Nalbuphine is similar in analgesic efficacy to morphine, but shows negligible respiratory effects.
source: Likewise, nalbuphine, a moderate efficacy MOR partial agonist and high efficacy KOR partial agonist (Schmidt et al., 1985; Peng et al., 2007), is similar in analgesic efficacy to morphine, but shows negligible respiratory effects (Schmidt et al., 1985)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Schmidt et al., 1985.

claim: Specific receptor-ligand interactions at the TM5-ECL2 region in the orthosteric ligand pocket may reduce arrestin recruitment at both MOR and KOR.
source: Comparative structural analysis and docking to opioid receptors, including the recent nanobody-stabilized active state KOR complexed with MP1104 (Che et al., 2018; Váradi et al., 2015a), suggested that specific receptor-ligand interactions at the TM5-ECL2 region in the orthosteric ligand pocket may reduce arrestin recruitment at both MOR and KOR (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is based on computational modeling and docking studies, with reference to Figure 1A.

claim: MP1207 and MP1208 displayed MOR/KOR Gi-partial agonism with diminished arrestin signaling.
source: The lead compounds, MP1207 and MP1208, displayed MOR/KOR Gi-partial agonism with diminished arrestin signaling, showed efficient analgesia with attenuated liabilities, including respiratory depression and conditioned place preference and aversion in mice.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: MP1207 and MP1208 showed efficient analgesia with attenuated liabilities, including respiratory depression and conditioned place preference and aversion in mice.
source: The lead compounds, MP1207 and MP1208, displayed MOR/KOR Gi-partial agonism with diminished arrestin signaling, showed efficient analgesia with attenuated liabilities, including respiratory depression and conditioned place preference and aversion in mice.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: MP1104 robustly recruits β-arrestin2 at mu and kappa opioid receptors.
source: Functional studies (cAMP and β-arrestin2 recruitment assays) showed that MP1104 robustly recruits β-arrestin2 at mu and kappa opioid receptors (Che et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Che et al., 2018.

claim: MP1104 has a bias factor of 0.58 at hMOR.
source: Its bias factors at hMOR and hKOR were determined to be 0.58 (Figure 2A–B and Appendix 1—figure 4B, Appendix 1—table 10) and 0.15 (Figure 2C–D and Appendix 1—figure 4A, Appendix 1—table 10), respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in figures and tables.

claim: MP1104 has a bias factor of 0.15 at hKOR.
source: Its bias factors at hMOR and hKOR were determined to be 0.58 (Figure 2A–B and Appendix 1—figure 4B, Appendix 1—table 10) and 0.15 (Figure 2C–D and Appendix 1—figure 4A, Appendix 1—table 10), respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in figures and tables.

claim: MP1104 is a full agonist in hMOR in cAMP inhibition compared to DAMGO.
source: MP1104 (red) is a full agonist in hMOR in cAMP inhibition (N = 5) and Tango-arrestin recruitment assays (N = 5) compared to DAMGO (blue).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A-B.

claim: MP1104 is a full agonist in hMOR in Tango-arrestin recruitment assays compared to DAMGO.
source: MP1104 (red) is a full agonist in hMOR in cAMP inhibition (N = 5) and Tango-arrestin recruitment assays (N = 5) compared to DAMGO (blue).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A-B.

claim: MP1104 is a full agonist in hKOR in cAMP inhibition compared to U50,488H.
source: MP1104 (red) is a full agonist in hKOR in cAMP inhibition (N = 3) and Tango-arrestin recruitment assays (N = 3) compared to U50,488H (purple).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C-D.

claim: MP1104 is a full agonist in hKOR in Tango-arrestin recruitment assays compared to U50,488H.
source: MP1104 (red) is a full agonist in hKOR in cAMP inhibition (N = 3) and Tango-arrestin recruitment assays (N = 3) compared to U50,488H (purple).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C-D.

claim: MP1104 was found to be arrestin biased at both mMOR and rKOR with bias factors of 0.11 and 0.23, respectively.
source: Confirming the cAMP inhibition assay and β-arrestin2 recruitment results obtained for human opioid receptors, MP1104 was found to be arrestin biased at both mMOR (Appendix 1—figure 1A and 4C, Appendix 1—table 11) as well as rKOR (Appendix 1—figure 2A and 4C, Appendix 1—table 11) with bias factors of 0.11 and 0.23, respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in appendix figures and tables.

claim: IBNtxA showed reduced β-arrestin2 recruitment at hMOR while recruiting β-arrestin2 through hKOR activity.
source: In contrast to MP1104, the closely related ligand IBNtxA (Majumdar et al., 2011a; Figure 1B) with a hydroxyl (C14-OH) group and a saturated ring C, showed reduced β-arrestin2 recruitment at hMOR while recruiting β-arrestin2 through hKOR activity (Appendix 1—figure 3A-D and 4A-B and Appendix 1—table 10, bias factor = 0.1 at hKOR and 24 at hMOR) (Che et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and citation to Che et al., 2018.

claim: IBNtxA has a bias factor of 0.1 at hKOR and 24 at hMOR.
source: In contrast to MP1104, the closely related ligand IBNtxA (Majumdar et al., 2011a; Figure 1B) with a hydroxyl (C14-OH) group and a saturated ring C, showed reduced β-arrestin2 recruitment at hMOR while recruiting β-arrestin2 through hKOR activity (Appendix 1—figure 3A-D and 4A-B and Appendix 1—table 10, bias factor = 0.1 at hKOR and 24 at hMOR) (Che et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and citation to Che et al., 2018.

claim: MP1202 was found to be G protein biased at hMOR with a bias factor of 31.
source: At human opioid receptors, MP1202 was similar to IBNtxA and was found to be G protein biased at hMOR (bias factor = 31, Figure 2G–H, Appendix 1—figure 4B and Appendix 1—table 10) while showing β-arrestin2 recruitment and arrestin bias at hKOR (Figure 2I–J, Appendix 1—figure 4A, and Appendix 1—table 10).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in figures and tables.

claim: MP1202 shows β-arrestin2 recruitment and arrestin bias at hKOR.
source: At human opioid receptors, MP1202 was similar to IBNtxA and was found to be G protein biased at hMOR (bias factor = 31, Figure 2G–H, Appendix 1—figure 4B and Appendix 1—table 10) while showing β-arrestin2 recruitment and arrestin bias at hKOR (Figure 2I–J, Appendix 1—figure 4A, and Appendix 1—table 10).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in figures and tables.

claim: MP1202 is a full agonist in hMOR in cAMP inhibition compared to DAMGO.
source: MP1202 (red) is a full agonist in hMOR in cAMP inhibition (N = 3) and partial agonist in Tango-arrestin recruitment assays (N = 3) compared to DAMGO (blue).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2G-H.

claim: MP1202 is a partial agonist in hMOR in Tango-arrestin recruitment assays compared to DAMGO.
source: MP1202 (red) is a full agonist in hMOR in cAMP inhibition (N = 3) and partial agonist in Tango-arrestin recruitment assays (N = 3) compared to DAMGO (blue).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2G-H.

claim: MP1202 is a full agonist in hKOR in cAMP inhibition compared to U50,488h.
source: MP1202 (green) is a full agonist in hKOR in cAMP inhibition (N = 3) and in Tango-arrestin recruitment assays (N = 3) compared to U50,488h (purple).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2I-J.

claim: MP1202 is a full agonist in hKOR in Tango-arrestin recruitment assays compared to U50,488h.
source: MP1202 (green) is a full agonist in hKOR in cAMP inhibition (N = 3) and in Tango-arrestin recruitment assays (N = 3) compared to U50,488h (purple).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2I-J.

claim: The unsaturated ring C of MP1104 strongly prefers the boat conformation.
source: Indeed, we found a strong preference for the unsaturated ring C of MP1104 to be in the boat conformation, based on analysis of similar ligands in the Crystallography Open Database and our quantum mechanics (QM) energy calculations.
evidence: The claim is based on computational analysis and QM calculations.

claim: The saturated C rings of both IBNtxA and MP1202 could assume both chair and boat conformations with only a modest preference for chair conformation.
source: At the same time, the saturated C rings of both IBNtxA and MP1202 could assume both chair and boat conformations with only a modest preference for chair conformation (Appendix 1—tables 3–4).
evidence: The claim is based on computational analysis shown in appendix tables.

claim: The amidophenyl moiety of MP1104 in both MOR and KOR occupied a sub-pocket between TM2 and TM3.
source: Due to the boat-form restriction for the unsaturated ring C, the amidophenyl moiety of the best-scored docking poses for MP1104 in both MOR and KOR occupied a sub-pocket between TM2 and TM3 (Figure 2E and F).
evidence: The claim is based on docking studies shown in Figure 2E and F.

claim: The best-scored IBNtxA and MP1202 docking poses in MOR consistently adopted the chair conformation of ring C.
source: However, we found that in MOR the best-scored IBNtxA (Appendix 1—figure 3E) and MP1202 (Figure 2K) docking poses consistently adopted the chair conformation of ring C, while in KOR the best-scored poses adopted the boat conformation (Appendix 1—figure 3J and Figure 2L).
evidence: The claim is based on docking studies shown in figures.

claim: The best-scored IBNtxA and MP1202 docking poses in KOR adopted the boat conformation.
source: However, we found that in MOR the best-scored IBNtxA (Appendix 1—figure 3E) and MP1202 (Figure 2K) docking poses consistently adopted the chair conformation of ring C, while in KOR the best-scored poses adopted the boat conformation (Appendix 1—figure 3J and Figure 2L).
evidence: The claim is based on docking studies shown in figures.

claim: MP1207 and MP1208 are G protein biased agonists at hKOR with bias factors of 8 and 22, respectively.
source: Functional studies using cAMP inhibition and Tango assays at human opioid receptors showed that both MP1207 and MP1208 are G protein biased agonists at hKOR with bias factors of 8 and 22 (Figure 3A–B, Appendix 1—figure 4A and Appendix 1—table 10), respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in figures and tables.

claim: At hMOR, recruitment of arrestin was completely abolished for both MP1207 and MP1208.
source: At hMOR, recruitment of arrestin was completely abolished for both ligands; however, reduction of cAMP inhibition was also observed, with Emax values of = 33% for MP1207 and 42% for MP1208 compared to DAMGO (Figure 3E–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E-F.

claim: MP1207 has Emax value of 33% in cAMP inhibition at hMOR compared to DAMGO.
source: At hMOR, recruitment of arrestin was completely abolished for both ligands; however, reduction of cAMP inhibition was also observed, with Emax values of = 33% for MP1207 and 42% for MP1208 compared to DAMGO (Figure 3E–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E-F.

claim: MP1208 has Emax value of 42% in cAMP inhibition at hMOR compared to DAMGO.
source: At hMOR, recruitment of arrestin was completely abolished for both ligands; however, reduction of cAMP inhibition was also observed, with Emax values of = 33% for MP1207 and 42% for MP1208 compared to DAMGO (Figure 3E–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E-F.

claim: MP1207 and MP1208 showed similar affinities at mMOR (Ki = 0.23 nM and 0.34 nM) and mKOR (Ki = 0.39 and 0.28 nM).
source: In binding assays, both MP1207 (m-amine group) and MP1208 (m-guanidine group) showed similar affinities at mMOR (Ki = 0.23 nM and 0.34 nM) and mKOR (Ki = 0.39 and 0.28 nM) with substantial selectivity over mDOR (Ki = 15.62 and 19.28 nM) (Appendix 1—table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in appendix table.

claim: MP1207 and MP1208 showed substantial selectivity over mDOR (Ki = 15.62 and 19.28 nM).
source: In binding assays, both MP1207 (m-amine group) and MP1208 (m-guanidine group) showed similar affinities at mMOR (Ki = 0.23 nM and 0.34 nM) and mKOR (Ki = 0.39 and 0.28 nM) with substantial selectivity over mDOR (Ki = 15.62 and 19.28 nM) (Appendix 1—table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in appendix table.

claim: MP1207 and MP1208 were partial agonists at both mKOR and mMOR in [35S]GTPγS binding assays.
source: In [35S]GTPγS binding assays both MP1207 and MP1208 were partial agonists at both mKOR and mMOR, still maintaining very high potency at mKOR (EC50 = 1.5 and 1.4 nM) and at mMOR (EC50 = 1.3 and 1.1 nM).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from GTPγS binding assays.

claim: MP1207 and MP1208 maintained very high potency at mKOR (EC50 = 1.5 and 1.4 nM) and at mMOR (EC50 = 1.3 and 1.1 nM) in [35S]GTPγS binding assays.
source: In [35S]GTPγS binding assays both MP1207 and MP1208 were partial agonists at both mKOR and mMOR, still maintaining very high potency at mKOR (EC50 = 1.5 and 1.4 nM) and at mMOR (EC50 = 1.3 and 1.1 nM).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from GTPγS binding assays.

claim: MP1207 and MP1208 show only weak efficacy at mDOR.
source: At mDOR both MP1207 and MP1208 show only weak efficacy (Appendix 1—tables 2 and 6).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in appendix tables.

claim: No recruitment of βarrestin-2 was seen with either MP1207 or MP1208 when rodent opioid receptors were used in BRET assays.
source: No recruitment of βarrestin-2 was seen with either MP1207 or MP1208 when rodent opioid receptors were used in BRET assays.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from BRET assays.

claim: MP1207 had a Ki >10 µM affinity at all screened targets except SERT and α2C-adrenoreceptors.
source: MP1207 had a Ki >10 µM affinity at all screened targets except SERT and α2C-adrenoreceptors, which displayed Ki (pKI± SEM) of 356 (6.45 ± 0.091)nM and 2979 (5.53 ± 0.16) nM respectively (Besnard et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from radioligand binding assays.

claim: MP1207 displayed Ki of 356 nM at SERT and 2979 nM at α2C-adrenoreceptors.
source: MP1207 had a Ki >10 µM affinity at all screened targets except SERT and α2C-adrenoreceptors, which displayed Ki (pKI± SEM) of 356 (6.45 ± 0.091)nM and 2979 (5.53 ± 0.16) nM respectively (Besnard et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from radioligand binding assays.

claim: MP1207 shows a 900-fold selectivity for MOR and KOR over the nearest non-opioid target.
source: At MOR, KOR, and DOR the respective values were 0.39 (9.4 ± 0.042), 0.39 (9.4 ± 0.056), and 60.1 (7.22 ± 0.059) showing a 900-fold selectivity for MOR and KOR over the nearest non-opioid target.
evidence: The claim is based on comparison of binding affinity data.

claim: Over 50% of the cumulative trajectory frames from the two 1000 ns long MD runs had distances between carboxylate oxygens of acidic residues within 4.5 Å of methyl amine nitrogen atom of MP1207.
source: Over 50% of the cumulative trajectory frames from the two 1000 ns long MD runs had distances between carboxylate oxygens of these acidic residues within 4.5 Å of methyl amine nitrogen atom of MP1207.
evidence: The claim is based on MD simulation data.

claim: The methyl amine of MP1207 can form salt bridge interactions with both E209ECL2 and D2235.35 residues.
source: The methyl amine of MP1207 can form salt bridge interactions with both E209ECL2 and D2235.35 residues, and during MD simulations a fluctuating switch between these two residues was observed.
evidence: The claim is based on MD simulation data.

claim: Y312W7.35 mutation in KOR reduced βarrestin-2 recruitment for IBNtxA.
source: Indeed, we had previously shown that a mutation of Y312W7.35 in the TM2-TM3 region of KOR reduces βarrestin-2 recruitment for IBNtxA, which has a similar amidophenyl arm (Che et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Che et al., 2018.

claim: Y312W7.35 mutation in KOR reduced arrestin recruitment by MP1202 to the level observed for MOR, resulting in strong G protein bias (bias factor = 34).
source: As expected, this mutation in KOR reduced arrestin recruitment by MP1202 to the level observed for MOR, resulting in strong G protein bias (bias factor = 34, Appendix 1—figure 7A&C and L) as opposed to robust β-arrestin2 recruitment in the wild-type KOR (Appendix 1—figure 7B and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in appendix figures.

claim: MP1209 and MP1210 lost their G protein bias in hKOR and showed no bias.
source: Consistent with our predictions (Appendix 1—table 4), the para-substituted and more planar analog, MP1209 and the meta substituted methyl hydroxyl analog (MP1210) which are incapable of forming a salt bridge with D2235.35 and E209ECL2, lost their G protein bias in hKOR and showed no bias (Figure 4C–D, Appendix 1—figure 4A and Appendix 1—table 10) while retaining hMOR null arrestin recruitment (Figure 4E–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in figures and tables.

claim: MP1209 and MP1210 retained hMOR null arrestin recruitment.
source: Consistent with our predictions (Appendix 1—table 4), the para-substituted and more planar analog, MP1209 and the meta substituted methyl hydroxyl analog (MP1210) which are incapable of forming a salt bridge with D2235.35 and E209ECL2, lost their G protein bias in hKOR and showed no bias (Figure 4C–D, Appendix 1—figure 4A and Appendix 1—table 10) while retaining hMOR null arrestin recruitment (Figure 4E–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: Methoxylcarbonyl fentanyl showed strong arrestin recruitment and arrestin bias (bias factor = 0.09 at hMOR).
source: We evaluated G protein/arrestin activity of both compounds and found that as expected, methoxylcarbonyl fentanyl showed strong arrestin recruitment and arrestin bias (bias factor = 0.09 at hMOR, Appendix 1—figure 8A-B, C-D and 8 and Appendix 1—table 10)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in appendix figures and tables.

claim: MP102 targeting TM5 was unable to recruit arrestin at human and mouse receptors.
source: while MP102 targeting TM5 was unable to recruit arrestin at human (Appendix 1—figure 8F-G) and mouse receptors (Appendix 1—figure 8H-I).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in appendix figures.

claim: MP1305 was found to be G protein biased at MOR and KOR at human receptors with a bias factor of 11 and 4, respectively.
source: Consistent with our docking predictions, MP1305 was found to be G protein biased at MOR and KOR at human receptors with a bias factor of 11 and 4, respectively (Appendix 1—figure 9A-D and 4A-B and Appendix 1—table 10)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in appendix figures and tables.

claim: MP1601 showed a preference for the arrestin pathway at hKOR (bias factor = 0.5).
source: while MP1601 behaved similar to IBNtxA and MP1202 and showed a preference for the arrestin pathway at hKOR (bias factor = 0.5, Appendix 1—figure 9E-F and 4A and Appendix 1—table 10) while being G protein biased at hMOR (Bias factor = 4, Appendix 1—figure 9G-H and 4B and Appendix 1—table 10).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in appendix figures and tables.

claim: MP1601 was G protein biased at hMOR (Bias factor = 4).
source: while MP1601 behaved similar to IBNtxA and MP1202 and showed a preference for the arrestin pathway at hKOR (bias factor = 0.5, Appendix 1—figure 9E-F and 4A and Appendix 1—table 10) while being G protein biased at hMOR (Bias factor = 4, Appendix 1—figure 9G-H and 4B and Appendix 1—table 10).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in appendix figures and tables.

claim: The antinociceptive ED50 value of MP1207 was 6.1 (4.1–8.9) nmol.
source: The antinociceptive ED50 (and 95% CI) values of MP1207 and MP1208 were 6.1 (4.1–8.9) nmol (Figure 5A), and 7.2 (5.0–10.2), nmol respectively
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The antinociceptive ED50 value of MP1208 was 7.2 (5.0–10.2) nmol.
source: The antinociceptive ED50 (and 95% CI) values of MP1207 and MP1208 were 6.1 (4.1–8.9) nmol (Figure 5A), and 7.2 (5.0–10.2), nmol respectively
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The antinociceptive ED50 of U50,488h was 8.8 (5.7–13.5) nmol.
source: comparable to that of the kappa agonist U50,488h, 8.8 (5.7–13.5) nmol, although slightly higher than the ED50 of morphine, 4.77 (1.49–28.8) nmol, icv.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: The antinociceptive ED50 of morphine was 4.77 (1.49–28.8) nmol, icv.
source: comparable to that of the kappa agonist U50,488h, 8.8 (5.7–13.5) nmol, although slightly higher than the ED50 of morphine, 4.77 (1.49–28.8) nmol, icv.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: MP1207 showed antinociceptive responses that peaked at 10 min, returning to baseline values 90 min later.
source: Both drugs showed antinociceptive responses that peaked at 10 min, returning to baseline values 90 min later for MP1207 (Figure 5B) and 60 min for MP1208 (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: MP1208 showed antinociceptive responses that peaked at 10 min, returning to baseline values 60 min later.
source: Both drugs showed antinociceptive responses that peaked at 10 min, returning to baseline values 90 min later for MP1207 (Figure 5B) and 60 min for MP1208 (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: MP1207/08 antinociception was significantly attenuated in both MOR KO and KOR KO mice.
source: MP1207/08 antinociception was found to be significantly attenuated in both MOR KO and KOR KO mice, but remained intact in DOR KO mice.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: MP1207/08 antinociception remained intact in DOR KO mice.
source: MP1207/08 antinociception was found to be significantly attenuated in both MOR KO and KOR KO mice, but remained intact in DOR KO mice.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: Both MP1207 and MP1208 failed to show either rewarding or aversive behavior in mice in a conditioned place preference paradigm at 100 nmol, icv.
source: Both MP1207 and MP1208 failed to show either rewarding or aversive behavior in mice in a conditioned place preference paradigm at the highest dose that could be tested given their solubility (100 nmol, icv,~15 x analgesic ED50 dose) (Figure 5F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Morphine showed place preference in a conditioned place preference paradigm.
source: In contrast, morphine (tested at ~5 x the analgesic ED50 dose) and U50,488h (~15 x analgesic ED50 dose) as expected showed place preference and place aversion, respectively (Figure 5F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: U50,488h showed place aversion in a conditioned place preference paradigm.
source: In contrast, morphine (tested at ~5 x the analgesic ED50 dose) and U50,488h (~15 x analgesic ED50 dose) as expected showed place preference and place aversion, respectively (Figure 5F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Administration of morphine icv or IP decreased respiratory rate.
